Hi, I'm Shusuke Ioku, a Ph.D. candidate in Political Science at the University of Rochester. I work on political economy, combining formal theory with micro-level data—historical and contemporary—to study how technology reshapes political strategy. Three questions organize my research: what are the strategic implications of algorithmic technology and artificial intelligence; when does political competition turn violent; and how does government develop, broadly defined.

On the first, I develop [a formal framework](research.qmd#verification-paper) for how AI-powered influence operations degrade what online communities collectively know. When a community defends itself with identity verification, it screens out fabricated voices at the price of silencing its best-informed members—so an influence operation can deplete collective knowledge without deploying a single fake. The paper is currently under review.

On conflict, I study how radical elites broke interwar Japan's democracy by [organizing violence through civic associations](research.qmd#fascist-paper) that circumvented both parties and the military, and how a shock to military technology—the accidental arrival of firearms in 1543—[remade territorial competition](research.qmd#military-paper) among Japan's warring rulers and drove centralization.

On the development of government, I examine how subjects' ability to [exit across competing rulers](research.qmd#exit-paper) disciplined extraction in Tokugawa Japan, why early medieval statebuilders [dismantled their own administrative apparatus](research.qmd#feudalism-paper) and set feudalism in motion, and how [hydraulic management](research.qmd#hydraulic-paper) shaped which early states endured.

Across these settings the common thread is strategic: rulers, elites, and ordinary people adapting to new technologies of information, violence, and extraction—and political order changing as a result.
